title: Remove all spaces from a string.
shortTitle: Remove All Spaces from a String

s1_definition.profdef: Removing all spaces from a string produces a new string that keeps every non-space character in its original order while dropping every space character. Because Java strings are immutable, you build the result in a StringBuilder by appending only the characters that are not spaces, then convert back to a string. The operation runs in linear time and linear extra space in the length of the input, and you can choose to strip only the ASCII space or all whitespace including tabs and newlines.
s1_definition.analogy: When Rajesh enters his bank account number into the National Bank of India app, he sometimes types it with spaces for readability, like two zero zero space one. Before the system uses it, those spaces must be scrubbed out so the number becomes one clean token. We walk along the text and copy across only the real characters, skipping every space, and we get back a tidy account number with no gaps.
s1_definition.oneliner: Build a new string with a StringBuilder, appending only non-space characters, since strings cannot be edited in place.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Removing all spaces from a string produces a new string that keeps every non-space character in its original order while dropping every space character. Because Java strings are immutable, you build the result in a StringBuilder by appending only the characters that are not spaces, then convert back to a string. The operation runs in linear time and linear extra space in the length of the input, and you can choose to strip only the ASCII space or all whitespace including tabs and newlines.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When Rajesh enters his bank account number into the National Bank of India app, he sometimes types it with spaces for readability, like two zero zero space one. Before the system uses it, those spaces must be scrubbed out so the number becomes one clean token. We walk along the text and copy across only the real characters, skipping every space, and we get back a tidy account number with no gaps.

**One line to remember:** Build a new string with a StringBuilder, appending only non-space characters, since strings cannot be edited in place.

sections.s2_technical:
Java strings are immutable, so you cannot delete characters from an existing string. Instead you create a StringBuilder, loop through each character of the input, and append the character to the builder only if it is not a space. At the end you call toString on the builder to get the cleaned result. This approach is linear in time and clear to read.

A key decision is what counts as a space. If you only want to remove the ordinary ASCII space, you compare the character against the space character directly. If you want to remove every kind of whitespace, including tabs, newlines, and carriage returns, you use `Character.isWhitespace`, which recognises all of them. In banking I usually strip all whitespace from identifiers like account numbers so that a pasted value with a hidden tab is still cleaned.

Beginners often reach for the regular expression form, calling `replaceAll` with a whitespace pattern. That works and is concise, but it compiles a pattern on every call and has more overhead than a simple loop, so for hot paths I prefer the explicit StringBuilder loop, and if I do use a regex I pre-compile the pattern once and reuse it.

Another tempting approach is `replace` with the space character and an empty string, which removes only the literal ASCII space in one call and is actually quite efficient; but it will not touch tabs or newlines, so it is only correct when you truly mean the single space character.

A senior point is to size the StringBuilder sensibly. By default it grows as needed, but if you know the input length you can pre-size it to the input length to avoid repeated internal array growth, which is a small but real optimisation for large strings processed at high volume, such as a bulk import of account identifiers.

One more subtlety is that trimming and removing-all-spaces are different. Trimming removes only leading and trailing whitespace and leaves inner spaces alone, while removing all spaces deletes every space anywhere. For an account number you want full removal, but for a display name you usually only want trimming, so I am careful to pick the right one.

A small finance-domain example: `StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(input.length()); for (int i = 0; i < input.length(); i++) { char c = input.charAt(i); if (!Character.isWhitespace(c)) sb.append(c); } String cleaned = sb.toString();` which turns "200 1" into "2001".
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, customers copy and paste account numbers and IFSC-style codes from emails and statements, and these pasted values frequently carry spaces, tabs, or line breaks. If the backend stores or looks up the value with those hidden characters, the lookup fails even though the human-readable number is correct. So before storing or matching, the system must scrub out every whitespace character. Removing all spaces is exactly this cleaning step.

This is exactly how remove-all-spaces works in Java — we copy only the real characters into a fresh string, dropping every whitespace.

Problem 2 — The same system must clean a bulk file where thousands of account identifiers are imported at once, so the cleaning routine must be efficient and must handle not only ordinary spaces but tabs and newlines pasted from spreadsheets. This means using the whitespace-aware check and pre-sizing the builder for speed on large input.

What the code will do: an `IdentifierCleaner` class with `removeSpaces(String s)` that strips only the ASCII space, and `removeAllWhitespace(String s)` that strips every whitespace using a pre-sized StringBuilder. The demo cleans Rajesh's spaced account number and a tab-laden pasted code.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's pasted account is `SAV 2001` and Priya's pasted code is `CUR`, a tab, `3001`, a newline.

Step 1: `removeSpaces("SAV 2001")` runs. The string is not null, so we create a StringBuilder pre-sized to the input length `8`.

Step 2: We loop character by character. `S`, `A`, `V` are not spaces, so each is appended, giving `SAV`. The next character is a space, so we skip it, appending nothing.

Step 3: We continue with `2`, `0`, `0`, `1`, all appended, giving `SAV2001`. The loop ends and toString returns `SAV2001`. The original string is untouched because strings are immutable.

Step 4: `removeAllWhitespace` runs on the pasted code. We create a pre-sized StringBuilder. We append `C`, `U`, `R`. The next character is a tab, which `Character.isWhitespace` recognises, so we skip it.

Step 5: We append `3`, `0`, `0`, `1`. The final character is a newline, which is also whitespace, so we skip it. The builder now holds `CUR3001`.

Step 6: toString returns `CUR3001`. Both cleaned values are now safe to store and to match against the database, with no hidden characters to cause a failed lookup.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T15:00:00Z INFO Rajesh account cleaned (spaces only): 'SAV2001'
2026-10-26T15:00:00Z INFO Priya pasted code cleaned (all whitespace): 'CUR3001'
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Removing all spaces from a string in Java means producing a new string, because strings are immutable and cannot be edited in place. I create a StringBuilder, loop over every character, and append only the characters that are not spaces, then convert back to a string. The whole thing is linear in the length of the input.

The decision I always make explicit is what counts as a space. If I only want to drop the plain ASCII space, I compare against the space character directly or use replace. If I want to drop every kind of whitespace, including tabs and newlines pasted from a spreadsheet, I use Character dot isWhitespace, which recognises them all. For banking identifiers I usually strip all whitespace so a value with a hidden tab is still cleaned.

I also distinguish removing all spaces from trimming: trimming only removes leading and trailing whitespace and keeps inner spaces, which is right for a display name, whereas full removal deletes every space anywhere, which is right for an account number. And on large or high-volume input I pre-size the StringBuilder to the input length to avoid repeated internal growth, and I avoid recompiling a regular expression on every call.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this when customers paste account numbers and codes from emails and statements, because those pasted values carry spaces, tabs, and line breaks that make a database lookup fail even when the human-readable number is correct. The cleaning step runs before storage and before matching, and the bulk-import path uses the whitespace-aware, pre-sized version. Explaining the trim-versus-remove distinction and the whitespace nuance shows the interviewer that I handle real, messy input rather than only tidy examples.
